38-004.r: Chambal Ravines → formed by Gully erosion (deep channels cut by running water).

38-005.r: Order of soil erosion process: Splash (raindrop) → Sheet → Rill → Gully.
38-005.h: Drop, sheet, small channel, deep channel: erosion grows from a raindrop to a gully.

38-006.r: Farmland erodes most rapidly when planted with Sorghum; Clover causes the least erosion (World Wildlife Fund analysis).

38-007.r: Seed modification does not raise soil fertility; crop rotation, mixed cultivation and multiple cropping do.

38-008.r: Crop rotation → increases soil fertility (same crop each season drains the same nutrients); also helps pest control.

38-009.r: Soil conservation methods in India (answer 1, 3, 4): crop rotation, terracing, windbreaks; sand fences not counted.

38-010.r: Soil erosion problem in India → linked to deforestation (answer: 2 only); terrace cultivation and tropical climate not counted.
38-010.t: Terracing is a soil conservation method, not a cause of erosion.

38-011.r: Soil erosion is checked/prevented by afforestation; also contour tillage and banning shifting cultivation.

38-013.r: Water conservation in farming: reduced/zero tillage, gypsum before irrigation (dissolves salt clay pan), leaving crop residue → all three help.

39-001.r: Birch tree → Himalayas; its white paper-like bark was used in ancient times for writing scriptures.

39-002.r: Katha → obtained from the wood of Khair (white substance in Khair wood).

39-003.r: Largest forest type in India: Tropical Dry Deciduous (39.22%); among the options, Tropical Moist Deciduous (second largest; teak, sal).
39-003.t: Don't confuse: dry deciduous is largest overall; moist deciduous is second and the answer only because dry was not an option.

39-004.r: Sal (Shorea robusta) → deciduous, not evergreen; Deodar, Silver fir, Blue pine are evergreen conifers. Teak and Sal → tropical deciduous forests.

39-006.r: Largest forest group in India → Tropical Dry Deciduous: 43.85% of all forest-group area, 8.53% of geographical area.

39-007.r: Himalayan vegetation changes with altitude due to: fall in temperature, change in rain forms, infertile soil (answer 1, 2, 3).

39-008.r: Himalayas have varied vegetation because climate changes with altitude → A and R true; R explains A.

39-009.r: Increasing soil loss: Splash → Sheet → Rill → Gully (II, IV, III, I).
39-009.h: Same order as the erosion process: drop, sheet, rill, gully.

39-010.r: Tree-line: Eastern/Central Himalayas about 3600-3800 m; Western/NW Himalayas about 3300-3600 m → lower in the West.

39-011.r: Major resource of Western Himalayan region → Forests (about 65% of the area).

39-012.r: Temperate zone of Western Himalayas (1500-2500 m) → Deodar most abundant (also Chir, Pine, other conifers).

39-013.r: Southern Himalayan slopes get more rain and sunlight → denser vegetation than northern slopes. So A false, R true.

39-014.r: Cinchona (evergreen tropical plant) → grows in Assam, Kerala, West Bengal; not in Chhattisgarh (dry/monsoon forests).

39-015.r: Flame of the forest → Butea monosperma (Dhak/Palash); Palash is the State Flower of Uttar Pradesh.

39-016.r: Teak forest (ISFR 2023) → found in Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh; maximum in Madhya Pradesh.
39-016.c: The book gives no single answer (*): teak occurs in three of the listed states; if one is needed, Madhya Pradesh (maximum).

39-017.r: Fern → no flowers and no seeds; reproduces by spores.

39-018.r: Alpine vegetation: up to 3000 m in western Himalayas, 4000 m in eastern → East is nearer the equator and sea coast (higher snowline).

39-019.r: Oryx → hot, arid areas; Chiru → steppes and semi-desert areas of cold high mountains.

39-020.r: Teak → Central India; Deodar → high Himalaya; Sundari → Sunderban, West Bengal (littoral/tidal forest); Cinchona → Himalayan Tarai.

39-023.r: Tropical moist deciduous → Tarai; Tropical dry deciduous → Middle Ganga Plain; Alpine → Arunachal Pradesh; Tropical evergreen → Sahyadris.

39-024.r: Tropical dry deciduous forests: neither statement true (not 25-75 cm rain, not a strip from Himalayan foot). Monsoon forests overall: 70-200 cm rain.

39-025.r: Tropical forest → Silent Valley; Conifer → Himachal Pradesh; Mangroves → Sunderbans; Deciduous → Rajasthan.

39-026.r: Tropical thorn forests (stunted, long roots, thorns) → rain under 70 cm, humidity under 50%, 25-30°C; e.g. Western Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Kutch.

39-027.r: Highest elevation among Deodar, Pine, Sal, Teak → Deodar (1500-3000 m, western Himalayas).

39-028.r: Wrong pair: Deodar — Nilgiri Hills (Deodar is a Himalayan conifer). Correct: Sal → NE Peninsula; Teak → western Peninsula; Sundari → Sundarban Delta.

39-029.r: 1997: Sal forests (marked 3 on the map) threatened by a severe epidemic of a tree pest.

39-030.r: Madhya Pradesh forests → classified as subtropical (tropical dry deciduous) forests.

39-031.r: Mahogany → not Himalayan; native to tropical America (West Indies, Central and South America). Juniper, Silver fir, Spruce are Himalayan.

39-032.r: Khejri → multipurpose social-forestry tree, 'king of the desert'; fuel, fodder, green manure; drought- and frost-resistant.

39-033.r: Victoria Falls → on Zambezi River, Zambia-Zimbabwe border (not Mozambique); 'The Smoke that Thunders'; World Heritage List 1989.

39-034.r: Lisa (resin) → from Pine trees of Uttarakhand; distilled into turpentine oil.

39-035.r: Mangroves: Achra Ratnagiri → Maharashtra; Coondapur → Karnataka; Pichavaram → Tamil Nadu; Vembanad → Kerala (not Karnataka).

39-037.r: Tropical rainforests in India → Kerala and Assam (Western Ghats, Andaman-Nicobar, upper Assam); best above 200 cm rain.

39-038.r: State with largest area under dense deciduous forest → Madhya Pradesh.

39-039.r: Bihar's largest dense forest district → Paschim (West) Champaran: 831.03 sq km (ISFR 2023); Kaimur 526 sq km.

39-040.r: Khair (Catechu) → sub-tropical forest tree (Shivalik and western Himalayas above 1000 m; with keekar, Acacia).

39-041.r: Highest percentage of area under forest (ISFR 2023) → Mizoram; so answer is 'None of the above'.

39-042.r: Sita Nadi Sanctuary (553.36 sq km, Chhattisgarh) → Sal dominant; its Sal forests rated the best in the country.

40-001.r: Pattiseema Lift Irrigation Project → links Godavari River to Krishna River.

40-002.r: Wrong pair: Jawai Project — Tamil Nadu; Jawai is in Rajasthan (Jawai River, Luni tributary). Ukai → Tapti, Gujarat; Ghatprabha → Karnataka; Nira → Maharashtra.

40-003.r: Ponds/tanks: major irrigation source in Peninsula (hard rock, uneven relief, seasonal rivers) → A and R true; R explains A.

40-004.r: Net irrigated area 2022-23: tube wells 49.34%, other wells 13.46%, canals 22.85%, tanks 2.82%, other sources 11.53%.
40-004.c: By the book's own data wells (49.34% + 13.46%) are the dominant irrigation source, so statement (b) is true and a doubtful answer to 'not correct'; many answer keys give (d) instead.
